chunks.title: Before helping anyone
chunks.text: Check that the area is safe for you before approaching an injured person. Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) for serious injuries. Wear gloves or use a plastic bag as a barrier if available when touching blood.

chunks.title: Bleeding
chunks.text: Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or bandage and keep pressing. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top without removing the first layer. Raise the injured arm or leg above heart level if it does not cause more pain. Seek medical help for deep wounds or bleeding that does not stop.

chunks.title: Cuts and wounds
chunks.text: Wash small cuts with clean water and soap, apply antiseptic, and cover with a clean bandage. Wounds from floodwater, rusty metal, or animal bites have a higher risk of infection and may need a tetanus shot or rabies care; see a health worker.

chunks.title: Burns
chunks.text: Cool the burn under cool, clean running water for about 20 minutes. Do not use ice, toothpaste, butter, or oil. Remove rings or tight items near the burn before swelling starts. Cover loosely with a clean, non-stick cloth or plastic wrap. Get medical help for large burns, burns on the face, hands, or genitals, or burns on children.

chunks.title: Possible broken bones
chunks.text: Do not try to straighten the injured part. Keep it still with a splint made from a board, rolled newspaper, or cardboard, padded with cloth and tied above and below the injury. Seek medical care.

chunks.title: Dehydration and heat exhaustion
chunks.text: Signs include thirst, dry mouth, dark urine, dizziness, weakness, and heavy sweating. Move the person to a cool shaded place, loosen clothing, and give small sips of water or oral rehydration solution. Heat stroke, with confusion, hot skin, or fainting, is an emergency: cool the person quickly with water and fanning and get medical help.

chunks.title: Unresponsive person
chunks.text: If a person does not respond and is not breathing normally, call 911 and start CPR if you are trained: push hard and fast in the center of the chest, about 100 to 120 times a minute. If the person is breathing, turn them on their side in the recovery position and stay with them until help arrives.

chunks.title: Warning signs of flooding
chunks.text: Heavy rain for many hours, rapidly rising rivers or creeks, and water entering streets are signs of possible flooding. Flash floods can arrive within minutes, especially near rivers and in low areas. If authorities issue a flood or rainfall warning for your area, prepare to move to higher ground.

chunks.title: Walking or driving through floodwater
chunks.text: Avoid walking or driving through floodwater. Just 15 centimeters (6 inches) of fast-moving water can knock an adult down, and about 60 centimeters (2 feet) can carry away a car. Floodwater can hide open manholes, sharp debris, and live electrical wires. If you must walk through water, use a stick to check the ground in front of you and walk where the water is not moving.

chunks.title: Electrical safety in floods
chunks.text: Turn off the main power switch before water enters the house, but only if you are standing on dry ground. Never touch electrical appliances, outlets, or switches while you are wet or standing in water. Stay away from fallen power lines and report them.

chunks.title: Health risks after floods
chunks.text: Floodwater is often contaminated with sewage and animal urine. Wading through it can cause leptospirosis, a serious infection that enters through cuts and the eyes, nose, or mouth. Wear boots if you must go through floodwater, wash with soap and clean water afterward, and see a health worker if you develop symptoms such as fever, muscle pain, headache, or red eyes in the following days.

chunks.title: Clean drinking water
chunks.text: Do not drink floodwater or water from flooded wells. Use bottled water, or boil water at a rolling boil for at least one minute before drinking. Throw away food that touched floodwater.

chunks.title: If you are trapped by rising water
chunks.text: Move to the highest floor or the roof. Do not enter a closed attic without a way out. Signal for help with a whistle, flashlight, or brightly colored cloth. Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) if you have a signal.

chunks.title: What a go-bag is
chunks.text: A go-bag (emergency bag) is a ready-packed bag you can grab immediately when you must evacuate. Prepare one per person, keep it light enough to carry while walking, and store it near the door. Check it every few months and replace expired food, water, and medicine.

chunks.title: Water and food
chunks.text: Pack drinking water, about 3 to 4 liters per person per day for at least 3 days if you can carry it, or as much as you can carry plus a way to get more. Pack ready-to-eat food that does not need cooking or much water: canned goods with pull-tab lids, crackers, biscuits, peanut butter, and energy bars. Include a manual can opener if cans need one.

chunks.title: Documents and money
chunks.text: Put copies of important documents in a waterproof plastic bag or envelope: valid IDs, birth certificates, insurance papers, land titles, and medical records or prescriptions. Bring some cash in small bills and coins because ATMs and card payments may not work during a brownout. Write down important phone numbers on paper in case your phone battery dies.

chunks.title: Light, power, and communication
chunks.text: Pack a flashlight and extra batteries, a whistle to signal for help, a fully charged power bank and charging cable, and a battery-powered or hand-crank radio to hear official announcements. Avoid using candles inside crowded evacuation areas because of fire risk.

chunks.title: Medicine and first aid
chunks.text: Pack a basic first aid kit: bandages, gauze, adhesive tape, antiseptic, alcohol or hand sanitizer, and pain or fever medicine. Bring at least a one-week supply of maintenance medicines, with a copy of the prescription. Include face masks, soap, and personal hygiene items.

chunks.title: Clothes and protection
chunks.text: Pack a change of clothes, a raincoat or poncho, a light blanket or emergency foil blanket, sturdy closed shoes or boots, and a cap or hat. Rubber boots help in flooded areas.

chunks.title: Infants and young children
chunks.text: For infants, pack diapers, wipes, baby formula or breast-milk storage supplies, clean bottles, safe drinking water for mixing formula, extra baby clothes, a blanket, and any baby medicines. Bring a familiar small toy or comfort item for young children. Keep a recent photo of each child and write your contact number on a card in their pocket in case you get separated.

chunks.title: Older adults, persons with disabilities, and pets
chunks.text: Pack extra maintenance medicine, eyeglasses, hearing-aid batteries, mobility aids, and adult diapers if needed. Write down medical conditions and doctor contacts. For pets, pack food, water, a leash or carrier, and vaccination records; ask in advance whether your evacuation site accepts pets.

chunks.text: For any emergency anywhere in the Philippines (police, fire, medical, rescue), call 911. It is the national emergency hotline. Source: DZRH News national hotline list, 7 January 2026.

chunks.title: Other towns and barangays
chunks.text: For other municipalities in the map area (Bauan, San Pascual, Ibaan, Rosario, San Jose, Cuenca, Alitagtag, Mabini, Tingloy and others), this device has no verified hotline list. Call 911, the Batangas PDRRMO, or your municipal hall. Your barangay hall and its Barangay DRRM Committee are usually the first responders for evacuation. Facility records on the map sometimes include a phone number from OpenStreetMap; treat those as unverified.

chunks.title: Preparing for brownouts
chunks.text: Keep flashlights and spare batteries where everyone can find them in the dark. Keep phones and power banks charged when power is available. Know how to reach your electric cooperative or utility to report outages.

chunks.title: Lighting safely
chunks.text: Use flashlights or battery LED lamps instead of candles or kerosene lamps when possible. If you must use a candle, put it in a stable holder away from curtains and children, and never leave it burning while you sleep.

chunks.title: Generators and carbon monoxide
chunks.text: Never run a generator, charcoal stove, or gas grill indoors or in a closed garage. They produce carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell that can kill. Keep generators outdoors and away from windows and doors. Signs of carbon monoxide poisoning include headache, dizziness, nausea, and confusion; move to fresh air immediately and seek medical help.

chunks.title: Appliances and power surges
chunks.text: Unplug sensitive appliances such as computers and TVs during an outage to protect them from surges when power returns. Leave one light switched on so you know when power is back. Do not overload extension cords when power returns.

chunks.title: Food safety without refrigeration
chunks.text: Keep the refrigerator and freezer doors closed as much as possible. A closed refrigerator keeps food cold for about 4 hours. Throw away perishable food such as meat, fish, eggs, and leftovers that have been above refrigerator temperature for more than 2 hours or that smell or look unusual.

chunks.title: Saving phone battery
chunks.text: Lower screen brightness, turn on battery saver, close unused apps, and turn off mobile data and Wi-Fi when you do not need them. Send text messages instead of calling when networks are congested, because texts need less network capacity.

chunks.title: Heat during outages
chunks.text: Without fans or air conditioning, drink water often, wear light clothing, and rest in the coolest shaded part of the house. Check on older adults, infants, and sick people, who are more affected by heat.

chunks.title: Before typhoon season
chunks.text: Know your area's hazards: flooding, landslides, and storm surge along the coast. Find out where your barangay's designated evacuation center is and walk the route in daylight. Prepare a go-bag for each family member and agree on a family meeting place and a contact person outside your area.

chunks.title: Understanding warnings
chunks.text: PAGASA issues Tropical Cyclone Wind Signals (TCWS) numbered 1 to 5 for specific areas. A higher number means stronger winds and less warning time. Signal No. 1: winds of 39 to 61 km/h expected within 36 hours, minimal to minor threat to lives and properties. Signal No. 2: 62 to 88 km/h within 24 hours, minor to moderate threat. Signal No. 3: 89 to 117 km/h within 18 hours, moderate to significant threat. Signal No. 4: 118 to 184 km/h within 12 hours, significant to severe threat. Signal No. 5: 185 km/h or higher within 12 hours, extreme threat to lives and properties. (Source: DOST-PAGASA press release on the modified TCWS system, 23 March 2022.) Listen for whether your province or municipality is included, and follow PAGASA, NDRRMC, and your local government on radio or TV. Saved information on this device cannot tell you the current signal level.

chunks.title: When a typhoon is approaching
chunks.text: Charge phones and power banks, fill containers with clean water, and stock food that does not need cooking. Secure or bring inside loose objects that strong winds can throw, such as roofing sheets, plants, and signs. Trim weak tree branches near the house if it is safe to do so. Move important items and electrical appliances to higher shelves in case of flooding.

chunks.title: When to evacuate
chunks.text: Evacuate immediately when local authorities order it, especially if you live in a low-lying, coastal, riverside, or landslide-prone area. Do not wait for water to rise. Bring your go-bag, turn off the main power switch and gas if you can do so safely, and lock your house.

chunks.title: During the typhoon
chunks.text: Stay indoors and away from windows and glass doors. Stay in the strongest part of the house. Do not go outside during the calm "eye" of the storm because strong winds return suddenly from the opposite direction. Keep listening to a battery-powered radio for updates.

chunks.title: After the typhoon
chunks.text: Wait for authorities to say it is safe before returning home. Watch for fallen power lines, damaged structures, and floodwater. Do not touch electrical lines. Check your house for damage before entering. Boil drinking water or use treated water if the supply may be contaminated.
